Island mackerel (Rastrelliger faughni) is a commercially important scombrid species found throughout the tropical waters of the Indo-Pacific region. Field surveys indicate that individuals attain a maximum body length of 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters], which corresponds to an ultimate wet weight of approximately 80 grams [Wwi = approximately 80 grams] based on length-weight relationships derived from local fisheries data. This relatively modest size is typical of smaller mackerel species within the genus Rastrelliger, contrasting sharply with the larger tunas and bonitos in the same family. The species exhibits rapid early growth, with the onset of sexual maturity occurring once individuals reach a total length of 10 centimeters [Lp = 10 centimeters]. At this developmental threshold, the average wet weight at puberty is recorded at 9.8 grams [Wwp = 9.8 grams], reflecting the allometric scaling between length and mass that characterizes this species during its juvenile-to-adult transition in warm coastal environments.

Reproductive output in Island mackerel has been characterized through gonad analyses and field observations of spawning aggregations, particularly under controlled thermal regimes. At a stable water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], females exhibit a maximum reproductive rate achieved by producing approximately 1 clutch annually [F_R_i = approximately 1 clutch annually], with each spawning event yielding a large batch of pelagic eggs. The estimated fecundity per reproductive event is approximately 34.5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 34.5 eggs per clutch], a figure derived from comparative studies with the closely related mackerel scad Decapterus macarellus. This annual reproductive strategy, characterized by the production of multiple moderate-sized egg batches, is consistent with the life-history patterns observed in other tropical scombrids inhabiting resource-predictable environments. The combination of protracted spawning seasons and relatively high fecundity per event likely buffers the population against recruitment failures caused by interannual variability in planktonic food availability.

Embryonic and larval development proceed rapidly under the warm conditions typical of the species' tropical habitat. At the same thermal regime of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], egg incubation concludes after approximately 4.5 days [ab = approximately 4.5 days], a brief period that is characteristic of small pelagic teleosts with high metabolic demands during early ontogeny. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge at a remarkably small size, with an estimated dry weight at birth of only 0.00045 grams [Wwb = 0.00045 grams], reflecting the minimal maternal investment per offspring in a species that produces numerous small, pelagic eggs. This dry mass corresponds to an egg diameter of approximately 0.95 millimeters, confirming the species' placement along the fast-life-history continuum. The rapid hatching time and diminutive larval size highlight the vulnerability of this early life stage to predation and starvation, as endotrophic reserves must sustain the prolarvae until mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding.

Longevity data for Island mackerel, compiled from otolith-based age estimates and mark-recapture studies conducted at a sustained temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], indicate that the maximum lifespan spans approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years]. This relatively short natural lifespan is typical of small, fast-growing, early-maturing scombrids that invest heavily in early reproduction rather than extended somatic persistence. The species reaches its asymptotic length of 20 centimeters within the first two years of life, after which growth slows considerably as the fish matures and resources are increasingly allocated to gamete production. The combination of a four-year maximum lifespan, rapid attainment of adult size, and early puberty at a length of only 10 centimeters exemplifies a life-history strategy geared toward high population turnover in productive tropical shelf ecosystems. Senescent individuals are rarely encountered in fishery landings, suggesting that natural mortality from predation and disease may truncate the realized lifespan below the theoretical maximum.

Comparative analyses with other members of the tribe Scombrini reveal that Island mackerel occupies a distinct ecological niche characterized by its small body size and rapid life-history pace. The ultimate wet weight of 80 grams [Wwi = 80 grams] and the corresponding body length of 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters] position this species near the lower end of the size spectrum within the genus Rastrelliger, with the closely related Indian mackerel (Rastrelliger kanagurta) attaining substantially larger dimensions. The wet weight at puberty of 9.8 grams [Wwp = 9.8 grams] and the total length at puberty of 10 centimeters [Lp = 10 centimeters] occur at a relatively early point in the lifespan, consistent with the species' elevated maximum reproductive output at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. These demographic parameters—rapid maturation, high fecundity, and abbreviated longevity—suggest that Island mackerel functions as a fast-turnover component of the pelagic fish community, likely playing a critical trophic role as both a zooplankton predator and a forage species for larger piscivores.
